messages.what: Here you can message other people who use the system, like a chat.
messages.example: you message a coworker to ask something without leaving the screen.

chatbot.what: It's an assistant that answers your questions about how to use the system, without needing to call anyone.
chatbot.example: you ask "how do I register a new client?" and it walks you through the steps.

notifications.what: Alerts you when something important happens: alerts, notices, requests waiting for your approval.
notifications.example: someone asks for authorization and the notice shows up here.

bookmarks.what: Saves your favorite screens so you can get back to them fast, without searching the menu every time.
bookmarks.example: you save the screen you use every day so you don't have to search for it again.

uiScale.what: Makes the text and tables bigger or smaller across the whole application.
uiScale.example: if reading is hard, you make it bigger; if you want to see more rows in a table, you make it smaller.

settings.what: This is where you change how the system looks and behaves for you: language, colors, and other options.
settings.example: you switch the language from English to Spanish, or the style from light to dark.

userInfo.what: Shows your personal information stored in the system, like your name and email.
userInfo.example: you check here if your email is spelled correctly.

businessProfile.what: Shows your information within the company: your position, your role, and who you report to.
businessProfile.example: you check here who your direct manager is in the system.

colSysEmpresa.what: Shows the name of the company this record belongs to.
colSysEmpresa.example: if you work across several companies in the system, this tells you which one this row is for.

colSysArea.what: Shows which area of the company this record belongs to, like Finance or Human Resources.
colSysArea.example: a payroll record usually shows "Human Resources" here.

colSysModulo.what: Shows which module or section of the system this record came from.
colSysModulo.example: if the record was created in "Supply Chain", it says that here.

colSysPantalla.what: Shows the exact name of the screen where this record was created.
colSysPantalla.example: if you filled it out in "Transfer Log", that name shows up here.

colSysCentroCostos.what: Shows which cost center this record belongs to, so you know who pays for it.
colSysCentroCostos.example: an expense from the North branch shows "North Branch" here.

colSysFecha.what: Is the exact date this record was saved, in the company's time zone.
colSysFecha.example: if you entered it today, you'll see today's date here, like "30/sep/2026".

colSysDiaNum.what: Is the day-of-month number when the record was saved.
colSysDiaNum.example: if it was saved on the 5th, this shows "05".

colSysDiaTexto.what: Shows which day of the week it was when the record was saved.
colSysDiaTexto.example: if it was a Monday, this shows "Mon".

colSysMesNum.what: Is the month number when the record was saved.
colSysMesNum.example: if it was September, this shows "09".

colSysMesTexto.what: Is the short month name when the record was saved.
colSysMesTexto.example: if it was September, this shows "Sep".

colSysAnio.what: Is the year the record was saved.
colSysAnio.example: if it was this year, this shows "2026".

colSysSemana.what: Shows which week of the year it was when the record was saved, to group information by week.
colSysSemana.example: if it was week 40 of the year, this shows "Sem40_2026".

colSysHora.what: Is the exact time, down to the second, the record was saved, in the company's time zone.
colSysHora.example: if you saved it at 3pm, this shows something like "15:04:22".

filterColumn.what: Lets you show only the rows that have a certain value in this column, instead of all of them.
filterColumn.example: in the "Status" column, you filter to see only the "Active" records.

zoomOut.what: Makes the table's text and rows smaller, so you can see more information at a glance.
zoomOut.example: if a table has many columns, you shrink it to see more without scrolling.

zoomIn.what: Makes the table's text and rows bigger, so it's easier to read.
zoomIn.example: if small numbers are hard to read, you make it bigger.

columnsEditor.what: Lets you choose which columns are shown, which are hidden and which stay pinned on the left side (up to 4), without deleting any of their information.
columnsEditor.example: you hide the columns you don't use and pin "Name" so you always know whose row it is, even looking at far-away columns.

saasAccessDialog.what: Here you choose what this account can see and do. If you check nothing, the account sees and does nothing: check only what it should have.
saasAccessDialog.example: you check “Our Plans” and the account sees that whole screen, with all its columns and buttons.

saasAccessCheck.what: This box gives or takes away this row's access for the account. If the row has things under it, checking it checks everything below; the dash means it only has part of it.
saasAccessCheck.example: you check “General” and the account gets Home, Dashboard, Search and the top icons that are Enabled.

saasAccessState.what: Shows how much of this row the account has: Full, Partial or No access (Yes or No for a single button or column). If it says “Being improved”, “Under construction” or “Disabled”, that row is not Enabled in the Master Tree and cannot be given to anyone yet.
saasAccessState.example: “Partial” on a screen means the account has some of its columns and buttons, but not all of them.

saasAccessAllNone.what: “All” checks everything under this row at once (only what is Enabled) and “None” removes it all. On a row with nothing under it, “All” grants that access and “None” removes it.
saasAccessAllNone.example: on “Customer Service”, “None” takes all of those screens away from the account at once.

saasAccessCount.what: How many of all the accesses in this row the account has. Anything not Enabled still counts in the total, but cannot be given.
saasAccessCount.example: “1/9” means it has 1 of the 9; the other 8 are not Enabled yet.

visibleStatuses.what: Here you choose which statuses this person can see. Anything not turned on stays invisible to them, even with the permission. Only the Test User needs all 4.
visibleStatuses.example: with only “Enabled” turned on, they do not see what is under construction or being improved.

breadcrumbRoute.what: Tells you where you are in the system: the places you went through to reach this screen. The names you can tap take you back to that place.
breadcrumbRoute.example: you are on “SaaS Team”; you tap “Home” and go back to the home screen without using the left menu.

breadcrumbToggle.what: The map that hides or shows the path above to give you more room on the screen. While the path is hidden, the name of the screen you are on stays here.
breadcrumbToggle.example: you tap the map and the path hides; you tap it again and it comes back.

sidebarCollapse.what: Shrinks the menu on the left so only its icons show and you get more room on the screen; tap it again and the menu opens fully.
sidebarCollapse.example: you tap the arrow, the menu gets narrow and the table gains room; you tap it again and the menu comes back.

topBarToggle.what: Hides or shows the bar at the top (the title and the icons) to give you more room on the screen.
topBarToggle.example: you tap it and the bar shrinks to a small arrow; you tap it again and it comes back.

screenTitle.what: The name of the screen you are on.
screenTitle.example: if it says “Welcome”, you are on the home screen; from there you reach the others with the menu on the left.

logout.what: Closes your session and takes you back to the sign-in screen. To use the system again you will have to type your username and password once more.
logout.example: you finish working on a shared computer, you tap “Log out” and nobody else can get in with your account.

sidebarMenu.what: The main menu on the left: from here you reach every screen in the system. Tap a screen name to open it, or the arrow at the top to shrink the menu.
sidebarMenu.example: you tap “SaaS Team” and that screen opens; you tap “Log out” at the bottom and leave the system.

brandRefresh.what: The logo and name at the top of the menu. Tapping it reloads the screen to bring the newest version of the system and shows “Update complete”.
brandRefresh.example: you are told there was an improvement, you tap the logo and the screen updates without closing the browser.

sidebarsToggle.what: Shows or hides the menu on the left on a phone screen, so the screen is less crowded.
sidebarsToggle.example: you are looking at a table on your phone, you tap this button and the menu hides; you tap it again and it comes back.

topBarActionsToggle.what: On a phone not all the icons at the top fit; this button gathers them into a list that opens when you tap it.
topBarActionsToggle.example: you tap the three dots and see Messages, Notifications, Settings and the other icons in a list.

masterTreeColorRequests.what: Shows the column color changes that were requested and are not applied yet: who asked, what the change is and who has to approve it. Whoever has permission can approve or reject them here.
masterTreeColorRequests.example: a person without permission to approve picks a color for “RFC”; it shows up here as pending and, once approved, the column is painted with that color.

masterTreeColorApprove.what: Approves this color change: it is applied on the real tables.
masterTreeColorApprove.example: you tap Approve and the “RFC” column changes to the color they asked for.

masterTreeColorReject.what: Rejects this color change: it is not applied and the column stays as it is.
masterTreeColorReject.example: the requested color does not match; you tap Reject and everything stays the same.

classOrigin.what: This column shows up in a different group than usual, and this says why: Own (this level changed it) or Inherits from a level above (Master, Business type, Plan, Client, Administrator, Profile). Only where it is shown changes; its permissions are the same.
classOrigin.example: "Inherits · Plan" on "Registration date" means the plan moved it to the "Dates" group.

limitsAuditRefresh.what: Checks the permissions of every client again with today's data.
limitsAuditRefresh.example: you fixed a client's contract; refresh and its count goes down.

limitsAuditTable.what: One row per client: how many of its users' permissions would break each limit (module not contracted, Status the user cannot see, outside the plan contract). A red number is what a blocking guard would stop allowing.
limitsAuditTable.example: a client with 12 under "Module not contracted" has users with permissions from a department it did not contract.

limitsAuditSamples.what: Shows or hides the per-user detail for this client: which Status they see, how many of their permissions break a limit and the exact reason, grouped (which Master Tree node is in which Status, which department is not contracted, which screens are outside the plan), with the most likely cause.
limitsAuditSamples.example: you see “Juan · 126 permissions: General is in Under improvement” and know you must change General’s Status or give Juan that Status.

systemResetBackup.what: Creates a full copy of the database and checks it (integrity and that it has every table). It is stored on the server and can be downloaded to your computer. Nothing can be deleted without a backup from the last hour.
systemResetBackup.example: before deleting, you create the backup, download it and keep it; if something goes wrong, that file recovers everything.

systemResetPreview.what: Shows how many records would be deleted per group and what is kept (Master Tree, business sectors, plans, SaaS team, catalogs). Display only: nothing is deleted here. The detail by table is below.
systemResetPreview.example: you see that 12 clients and 40 client users would be deleted, and that the 3 plans are kept.

systemResetRun.what: Permanently deletes the records in the list and leaves the configuration. It asks for three things: a backup from the last hour, typing the exact phrase, and the ALLOW_SYSTEM_RESET=true variable set in Railway (set it only while you use it and remove it afterwards). The numbering of what was deleted starts over and every session is closed at the end.
systemResetRun.example: before launching the system, you delete the tests so the first real client is client number 1.

changeHistory.what: Shows who changed something in this table, what they changed, and when: the date is in your local time and, below it, the base time (UTC) it is stored with.
changeHistory.example: if a value changed and you don't know why, this shows who modified it and what it used to be.

columnLegend.what: Explains what each color on the table means, what each of its icons does, and how what you type in the filters is read.
columnLegend.example: a green row can mean that record is editable, and below you see what each toolbar icon is for and what happens if you type several words separated by commas.

fieldRules.what: This is where you set the order this table's fields must be filled in, and which ones are required.
fieldRules.example: you require "Name" to be filled in before "Email" can be typed.

sidebarUserCard.what: Shows who is signed in: your name, your account type and, for a test account, the "Test" tag.
sidebarUserCard.example: if you switch from one account to another, this confirms which one you are working with before you save anything.

sidebarSearch.what: Searches for any screen in the menu by its name, without having to open every group to find it.
sidebarSearch.example: you type "transfer" and it shows you the Transfer Log screen directly.

edit.what: Opens this record so you can change its information.
edit.example: if a client's name is misspelled, you fix it here.

activate.what: Turns this record back on so it works in the system again, without having to create it from scratch.
activate.example: you reactivate a client who had stopped paying and is now caught up.

deactivate.what: Turns this record off without deleting it, so it stops working in the system for now.
deactivate.example: you deactivate a client who stopped paying, without losing any of their information.

adminAccess.what: Shows this client's main administrator username and password, so you can log into their account if you need to.
adminAccess.example: if the client asks for help and can't log in, you check their access details here.

permisosAdicionales.what: This is where you give a client extra access that wasn't included in their original plan, billed separately.
permisosAdicionales.example: a client wants a screen their plan doesn't include, you add it here and it gets added to their monthly payment.

appToggle.what: Turns this client's access to the mobile app on or off, without affecting their access to the web version.
appToggle.example: a client who only pays for Web shouldn't be able to use the App -- this is where you allow or remove it.

clientReset.what: Erases all of this client's test data and leaves it like new, so someone else can try it from scratch.
clientReset.example: you use this after a demo, to leave the test client clean for the next person.

resetTraining.what: Deletes this client's Training account's own practice records (the one they use to learn the system), without touching their real account or real data.
resetTraining.example: the client's team finished practicing and wants to start over, without deleting anything they're actually using for real.

delete.what: Removes this record from the system completely -- it can't be recovered afterward.
delete.example: you delete a plan you created by mistake that was never used.

planTree.what: This is where you set which screens and permissions this plan includes, and what it costs a client who subscribes to it.
planTree.example: you build a "Basic" plan with only 3 screens, and a "Premium" plan with all of them.

giroAccesosGlobales.what: Sets which screens and permissions every client in this business sector gets by default, without configuring each client one by one.
giroAccesosGlobales.example: every "Restaurants" client automatically sees the Food Inventory Control screen.

sectorCostAdjust.what: Sets the discount or increase this Giro (or Plan) applies on top of the Árbol Maestro's base cost -- one default for the whole tree, plus per-node exceptions if needed.
sectorCostAdjust.example: a screen's base cost is $100; if the Giro has a -10% default, that screen costs $90 for any plan under that giro, unless it has its own exception.

giroReordenPersonalizado.what: Changes the order and classification of screens and columns, only for clients in this business sector. If you can't authorize, it is sent as a request.
giroReordenPersonalizado.example: you move "Recipes" to the top of the menu because that's the first thing restaurants use.

clienteReordenPersonalizado.what: Changes the order and classification of screens and columns, only for the people of this client (its administrator, profiles and users). If you can't authorize, it is sent as a request.
clienteReordenPersonalizado.example: for "Transportes del Norte" you move "Fuel" to the top because it is the only thing they use every day; the other clients on its plan don't see that change.

perfilReordenPersonalizado.what: Changes the order and classification of screens and columns for the people who hold this position. If you can't authorize, it is sent as a request to your boss.
perfilReordenPersonalizado.example: for the "Accountant" position you move "Invoices" to the top of the menu; what the administrator set for everyone does not change.

usuarioReordenPersonalizado.what: Changes the order and classification of screens and columns only for this person. If you can't authorize, it is sent as a request to your boss.
usuarioReordenPersonalizado.example: for Ana you move "Invoices" to the top of the menu because she uses it the most; the rest of her position does not see it.

adminReordenPersonalizado.what: Changes the order and classification of screens and columns for this client's administrator and the levels below (profiles and users). If you can't authorize, it is sent as a request.
adminReordenPersonalizado.example: for the administrator of "Transportes del Norte" you move "Fuel" to the top; what the client set for everyone does not change.

planReordenPersonalizado.what: Changes the order and classification of screens and columns, only for clients on this plan. If you can't authorize, it is sent as a request.
planReordenPersonalizado.example: on the "Basic" plan you put "Invoices" first in the menu because that's what those clients use the most.

layoutResetOne.what: Removes this column's own classification and goes back to inheriting the one from the level above.
layoutResetOne.example: you changed "Plates" to another classification and regret it: you tap it and it goes back to what the level above sets.

layoutResetAll.what: Removes everything this level changed in order and classification and goes back to inheriting the level above's (a plan goes back to its business sector's; a client, to its plan's). Asks for confirmation.
layoutResetAll.example: you moved several lists and don't like how it turned out: you press it and everything goes back to the original order.

businessSectorPreview.what: Lets you see the system the way a client in this business sector would, without having to log in as one of them.
businessSectorPreview.example: you check what the menu looks like for a "Restaurants" client before activating it.

saasEditName.what: Changes the display name shown for this SaaS team account.
saasEditName.example: you fix "Admin" to show the person's real name, like "John Smith".

saasEditUsername.what: Changes the username this person logs in with.
saasEditUsername.example: you change "admin" to "john.smith" so each account is easier to tell apart.

saasAccountAccess.what: Sets which screens and what this person can do inside GEIPSA's admin panel.
saasAccountAccess.example: you give a sales person access to only "Nuestros Clientes", without seeing the rest.

saasResetPassword.what: Generates a new password for this account, in case the person lost or forgot theirs.
saasResetPassword.example: someone can't log in because they forgot their password, you reset it and share the new one.

download.what: Downloads this file to your computer so you can open or save it.
download.example: you download last month's database backup to review it.

evidencePhoto.what: This is where you upload or check a photo as proof of this data.
evidencePhoto.example: you upload a photo of the gas station receipt as proof of how much fuel was loaded.

hrActivateUser.what: Creates the username and password so this worker can log into the system for the first time.
hrActivateUser.example: you hire someone new and give them system access with this button.

hrResetPassword.what: Generates a new password for this worker, in case they lost or forgot theirs.
hrResetPassword.example: an employee can't remember their password, you reset it and share the new one.

jobPositionPermissions.what: Sets which screens and what anyone with this job position can do.
jobPositionPermissions.example: you give "Payroll" access to everyone with the "HR Manager" position, without setting up each person separately.

authorizeFieldRule.what: Activates this fill-order rule so it actually starts applying in the system.
authorizeFieldRule.example: someone creates a new rule, but it doesn't work until an administrator authorizes it here.

operationalStatusLocked.what: This user is automatically locked by their HR Status (for example, terminated); it can't be activated or deactivated by hand from here.
operationalStatusLocked.example: if someone was terminated in HR, this shows locked until it's resolved from their HR record.

activePermissionsTree.what: Shows a summary of everything this person can currently see and do, combining their job position and any extra permissions.
activePermissionsTree.example: you quickly check what an employee can do without reviewing every permission one by one.

grantAccess.what: Gives this person an extra permission that isn't included in their job position.
grantAccess.example: you give access to a special report to someone who wouldn't normally have it based on their position.

resetRole.what: Removes every extra permission you gave this person, leaving them with only what their job position normally includes.
resetRole.example: someone changed positions and you want to remove the extra access from their previous one.

reportRemoveColumn.what: Removes this column from the report you're building, without affecting the original data.
reportRemoveColumn.example: you added one extra column to the report, you remove it before saving.

reportRemoveOperand.what: Removes this value from the formula you're building for a calculated column.
reportRemoveOperand.example: you remove a number you no longer need in your formula's calculation.

reportAuthorize.what: Approves this report so it can actually run.
reportAuthorize.example: someone builds a new report, but it doesn't run until an administrator authorizes it here.

orgChartAltSupervisors.what: This is where you choose who can supervise this position besides its direct boss, for when that boss isn't available.
orgChartAltSupervisors.example: if the manager is on vacation, an alternate supervisor can approve things in their place.

masterTreeStatus.what: Says whether this screen, column or button is ready to use (Enabled), turned off (Disabled), or still being built (Under construction/Being improved).
masterTreeStatus.example: you set a new screen to "Disabled" while you finish it, so nobody sees it until it's ready.

masterTreeWeb.what: Turns this screen or feature on or off for the desktop (browser) version of the system.
masterTreeWeb.example: if you turn Web off for a new screen, nobody sees it on their computer until you turn it on.

masterTreeApp.what: Turns this screen or feature on or off for the mobile app, without affecting the desktop version.
masterTreeApp.example: a screen can be ready on Web but not yet on the App, until you turn on this switch.

masterTreeApplyNestedPlatform.what: Copies this same Web or App value to everything nested underneath, instead of checking each one by hand.
masterTreeApplyNestedPlatform.example: you turn Web on for "Customer Service" and apply it to all its screens in one click.

masterTreeApplyNestedStatus.what: Copies this same Status to everything nested underneath, instead of changing each one by hand.
masterTreeApplyNestedStatus.example: you set "Under construction" on a whole department and apply it to all its screens at once.

masterTreeClassification.what: Groups this column with others of the same kind (for example, every "Control Interno" or "Acciones" column), so they can share a color or be managed together.
masterTreeClassification.example: you group several columns as "Financial" so they're all painted the same color in the real table.

masterTreePreview.what: Shows you what this real screen looks like, without leaving the permission tree to go find it.
masterTreePreview.example: you quickly check what "Nuestros Clientes" looks like while deciding whether to enable it.

masterTreeAppVision.what: Marks whether this row also applies to the mobile version, in addition to web.
masterTreeAppVision.example: you check this box so a cost also applies in the App, not just on the computer.

masterTreeEqualizeRow.what: Copies this row's Web value over to the same row in App, so both end up the same.
masterTreeEqualizeRow.example: you set the same cost on Web and App without typing it twice.

permTreeLimitLock.what: A padlock on a checkbox means that permission cannot be given: it is not part of what the company contracted (plan and extras) or it is in a Status your account does not see. The checkbox stays off and “select all” skips it. If it was already granted before, you can remove it but not put it back.
permTreeLimitLock.example: a screen the company did not contract shows a padlock, and when you select the whole department the rest is checked and that one stays unchecked.

masterTreeFillMissingRow.what: Copies the Web value over to App only on rows where App is still empty, without touching the ones that already have their own value.
masterTreeFillMissingRow.example: you fill in every missing App cost at once, without overwriting the ones you already set differently.

masterTreeColumnColor.what: Changes the background and text color this group's columns use in the real table, so you can spot them at a glance.
masterTreeColumnColor.example: you make every "Por Definir" column yellow so they stand out among the rest.

masterTreeColorViewToggle.what: Shows a preview of what the real table would look like with this color applied, before saving it.
masterTreeColorViewToggle.example: you test a color before applying it, to check the text still reads well on top of it.

masterTreeColorReset.what: Removes the custom color and returns this column to its classification's default color.
masterTreeColorReset.example: you tried a color you didn't like and remove it with this button without having to remember the original.

paletteSeed.what: Here you pick one color that represents your brand, and the system automatically builds every other color from it.
paletteSeed.example: you pick your logo's blue, and the system suggests the rest of the colors (background, text, borders) that go well with that blue.

paletteSuggest.what: Regenerates every color in the system (background, text, borders, etc.) from the color you picked above, instead of adjusting each one by hand.
paletteSuggest.example: you change your brand color and use this button to update the whole system in one click.

palettePreviewTabs.what: Switches the sample screen in the preview: Home, as it looks on entering, or a data-entry table.
palettePreviewTabs.example: you look at Home to check the sidebar and the top bar, and at the table to check how rows and column titles turn out.

palettePreviewLegend.what: Lists each palette color with the place on the screen where it is used. Hovering one marks it on the sample screen.
palettePreviewLegend.example: you hover "Accent" and the sidebar header and the active menu option get marked.

paletteShowPreview.what: Shows or hides an example of what the real system would look like with these colors applied.
paletteShowPreview.example: you check the preview before saving, to confirm the colors look good together.

paletteEditColor.what: Opens the color palette so you can change this particular color: pick a theme color, a standard one, a recent one, or any other from "More colors...".
paletteEditColor.example: the background color turned out too dark, so you open it here and pick a lighter one.

mobileNewRecord.what: Creates a real, blank record right away -- not a form you fill out before saving. You fill in each field one at a time, and it saves as you go.
mobileNewRecord.example: you tap it to start a new record, then fill in each field one by one, without having to finish everything in one sitting.

mobileBarcodeScan.what: Opens the camera to scan the barcode, instead of typing it by hand.
mobileBarcodeScan.example: you point the camera at the box's barcode and the number fills in by itself.

roleEqualizeAllAppWeb.what: Copies the Web value over to App in EVERY row of this job position at once, instead of equalizing them one by one.
roleEqualizeAllAppWeb.example: you granted Web-only access to many screens, and with one tap you equalize them in App too.

roleFillMissingAppWeb.what: Copies Web over to App only in rows where App is still empty, without touching the ones you already set differently on purpose.
roleFillMissingAppWeb.example: you fill in every missing App permission at once, without overwriting the ones you already left different.

businessLogoUpload.what: This is where you upload your company's own logo, so it shows up in the system instead of the generic one.
businessLogoUpload.example: you upload your restaurant's logo so it shows at the top of the system instead of GEIPSA's.

businessLogoRemove.what: Removes the logo you uploaded and goes back to the generic one.
businessLogoRemove.example: you uploaded the wrong logo by mistake, and remove it here without having to find the right file yet.

sidebarNavigation.what: Takes you to that screen in the system.
sidebarNavigation.example: you tap a screen's name in the menu to open it.

layoutEmpty.what: Here you will see the map of your distribution center, with its zones, racks and cabinets, and their sizes in m² and m³.
layoutEmpty.example: you see on the map where rack A-R03 is and how much space it takes.

layoutKpis.what: A summary of the square meters of your warehouse: total, offices, aisles, docks, storage zones and dead space. Dead space is all the floor that has no zone: the total minus the m² already defined. It updates by itself every time you change the Layout.
layoutKpis.example: you define a 100 m² zone and the dead space goes down by 100 m².

layoutCargarPlano.what: Upload the floor plan of your warehouse, as an image or PDF, and draw the spaces on top of it.
layoutCargarPlano.example: you upload the plan the architect gave you and mark the zones and racks.

layoutCrearDesdeCero.what: Start without a plan: you enter the outline of the warehouse, its doors and power connections, and the system draws the map.
layoutCrearDesdeCero.example: you type that the warehouse is 48 by 28 meters and the map appears by itself.

verificadorSkuEmpty.what: Search or scan a code (SKU, UPC or description) to see which article it is and where it is. A barcode reader types into the field like a keyboard.
verificadorSkuEmpty.example: you scan the UPC of a box and see which article it is and on which rack, level and slot it is.

verificadorFicha.what: The article card: its descriptions, unit, type, measurements, weights and the 7 categories. Empty values show a dash.
verificadorFicha.example: you see it is a 4 × 11 × 6 cm box of the Medicine category.

verificadorUbicacion.what: The places where this code is, taken from Code Relation: one line per place, with the full route from cost center down to slot. "Located" means the exact slot is known (or it is a virtual sub-warehouse); "Partial" means it still needs completing.
verificadorUbicacion.example: it is in CEDIS Monterrey › General Warehouse › Medicines › Zone 1 › R-01 › Level 2 › Slot 3.

layoutSteps.what: The steps to build the Layout, like layers. Tap a step to see it on the sketch and edit it: only the step you tapped shows below. You can keep several on at once and the sketch shows the outline plus all of them. To hide a step, tap it again while it is the one you are editing.
layoutSteps.example: you tap Doors and then Power connections: you see both on the sketch and edit only the power below; you tap Doors again to edit the doors.

layoutSec_contorno.what: The corners of the warehouse in meters, with the height of each one, and the columns or obstacles. The total m² come from here and, with the heights, the m³.
layoutSec_contorno.example: a warehouse with a higher roof on one side has 6 meters at two corners and 10 at the other two.

layoutSec_puertas.what: The doors of the warehouse: which wall they are on, how many meters from the corner and how big they are.
layoutSec_puertas.example: the receiving dock is on wall 1, 6 meters from the corner, and is 3.5 wide.

layoutSec_luz.what: The electrical panels and outlets of the warehouse: which wall, how far from the corner and how high from the floor.
layoutSec_luz.example: a 220 V outlet on wall 3, 20 meters from the corner and 1.2 meters from the floor.

layoutSec_zonas.what: The zones of the warehouse: storage, docks, offices and aisles. The office and aisle m² come from here.
layoutSec_zonas.example: you define Zone A, dry goods, 22 by 11 meters.

layoutSec_espacios.what: The racks, cabinets and pallets, with their code, place and size. The storage m² and m³ come from here.
layoutSec_espacios.example: you register rack R-01, 3 by 1.1 meters, 4.5 high and 4 levels.

layoutLocked.what: This section cannot be changed with your current access.
layoutLocked.example: you can see the doors but not change them because you do not have the Modify permission.

layoutAddRow.what: Adds a new row to this list.
layoutAddRow.example: you add a new door for staff access.

layoutRemoveRow.what: Removes this row from the list. Nothing is deleted until you save.
layoutRemoveRow.example: you remove a door you entered by mistake.

layoutToggleRow.what: Deactivates or reactivates a zone or space that was already saved. It is not deleted: it stops counting in the m² and its history is kept.
layoutToggleRow.example: you deactivate a rack that was removed from the warehouse.

layoutDeleteRow.what: Permanently deletes this zone or space when you save. Unlike Deactivate, it is not kept at all. It only appears if your account has the Delete permission in the access tree.
layoutDeleteRow.example: you remove a rack that never existed in the warehouse and was entered by mistake.

tplButton.what: Creates many articles at once: you download an Excel template, fill it in and upload it (or paste the rows copied from Excel). Every row is checked before loading and errors are fixed right there.
tplButton.example: you load 40 new codes at once instead of one by one.

tplDownload.what: Downloads the Excel template with the article columns and an Instructions sheet with what goes in each one (and the catalog options). Only the UPC is required; the 6 photos are not part of the template.
tplDownload.example: you fill it in on your computer with the supplier data.

tplUpload.what: Uploads the .xlsx (or .csv) file with the rows. The first sheet and the headers it recognizes are read; up to 500 rows per load.

tplPaste.what: Paste the cells you copied from Excel, with the header row. It does the same as uploading the file.
tplPaste.example: you copy 20 lines in Excel and paste them here.

tplReview.what: Each line is a row of your file. What is in red has an error and its reason is on the right: type it correctly right there and the row becomes "Ready". Rows with errors are not loaded.
tplReview.example: you replace the repeated UPC with the right one and the row becomes Ready.

tplNext.what: Moves the cursor to the first field with an error that is still not fixed.
tplNext.example: you go through the errors one by one.

tplLoad.what: Creates the rows that are ready. The ones you did not fix or removed are not loaded and you can download them in an Excel with their reason. The new articles have no QR code until they have their 6 photos and all their data, just like the ones entered by hand.
tplLoad.example: you load 18 of 21 rows and download the 3 with errors.

relCodeSearch.what: Finds the code you will locate by its SKU (with or without zeros), UPC or description. It lists the codes from Article Setup.

relCostCenter.what: The cost center this place of the code belongs to. The list comes from Contracted Service.

relWarehouse.what: The warehouse of that cost center. Only the active warehouses of the chosen center appear.

relSubWarehouse.what: The sub-warehouse of that warehouse. It is optional: without it the relation stays "Partial".

relZone.what: The Layout zone it is in. Only the zones assigned to that sub-warehouse appear, and only if it is Physical.

relRack.what: The rack of that zone. If the sub-warehouse was assigned only some racks, only those appear.

relLevel.what: The level of the rack, from the bottom up. Each rack has the levels the Layout says.

relSlot.what: The slot inside that level. Each rack has the slots per level the Layout says, and each slot can hold only one code.

relPath.what: The full route built from what you choose, from cost center down to slot.
relPath.example: CEDIS Monterrey › General Warehouse › Medicines › Zone 1 › R-01 › Level 2 › Slot 3.

relSave.what: Saves the relation. With the cost center and warehouse it can already be saved; the rest is completed later.
relSave.example: You save with just the warehouse and later edit to add the rack.

relEdit.what: Changes the location of this row in the same window. Each field needs its own leaf in the tree.
relEdit.example: Move the code from level 2 to level 3.

whCostCenter.what: The cost center this warehouse belongs to. The list comes from Contracted Service.

whParentWarehouse.what: The warehouse this sub-warehouse belongs to. Only active warehouses are offered.

whKind.what: Physical: it exists in the building and gets Layout zones or racks assigned. Virtual: it takes no room in the building, for example goods in transit or on consignment.
whKind.example: Medicines is physical; In transit is virtual.

whLocationBtn.what: Assigns this sub-warehouse the whole zones or the Layout racks that belong to it. A zone or a rack can belong to only one sub-warehouse.
whLocationBtn.example: Medicines: all of Zone 1. Dressings: racks B-01 and B-02 of Zone 2.

whZoneAll.what: Marks the whole zone: all its racks stay in this sub-warehouse.

whRackCheck.what: Marks only this rack; the rest of the zone can belong to another sub-warehouse.

layoutZoneCats.what: Opens this zone's categories: the zone is the title and it holds its categories inside (several if there are different products), each with a name, short description, icon, color and its QR.
layoutZoneCats.example: Zone 1 holds Stationery and Solutions; another zone holds Brand, Generic and Antibiotic.

layoutCatName.what: The category name as it will show on the card and when its QR is scanned.

layoutCatDesc.what: A short description shown under the name on the card.

layoutCatLook.what: Changes the icon and color of this category. The color is the bar and the square of its row on the card.

layoutCatAdd.what: Adds another category to this zone. If the same zone holds another product with another category, the zone carries both.
layoutCatAdd.example: the Medicines zone also holds Solutions: you add the second category.

layoutCardBtn.what: Opens this zone's printable card: "Categories of" and the zone name, and for each category its icon, name and QR. It is built from what was last saved and has the same free size and dashed cut line as the Layout sheet.
layoutCardBtn.example: you print it on half letter, cut along the dashed line and stick it in the zone.

layoutSheetSize.what: The width and length, in centimeters, of the area you print. The sheet fits itself to that size (landscape, portrait or small) and the PDF and image come out the same. If the area is smaller than a page, the file comes out on the smallest standard page that fits with the area marked by a dashed cut line. From 6 to 120 cm per side.
layoutSheetSize.example: you type 10.5 by 14.8 for a card: it comes out on a Letter page with the card drawn with a dashed line, ready to cut.

layoutMeasures.what: Shows or hides the measures on the sketch: the length of each wall, the height of each corner and the measure of each zone side. The name and m² of each zone stay (to remove the m² use the icon next to it). The downloaded sheet comes out as you see it; the public QR view does not change.
layoutMeasures.example: you hide the measures when the sketch looks crowded with numbers and show them again to check a side.

layoutArea.what: Shows or hides the m² under each zone name on the sketch. The name stays. The downloaded sheet (PDF or image) comes out as you see it; the public QR view does not change and the zones table still shows the surface.
layoutArea.example: you hide the m² so the sketch only shows the zone names and show them again to check how big each one is.

layoutSheetContent.what: Choose what the downloaded sheet carries: the measures (length of each wall, corner heights and the measure of each zone side), the m² of each zone and the totals (the m² and m³ figures at the bottom: total area, offices, aisles, storage, dead space and volume). When off, that part is not printed and the sketch takes its place. It only changes this download: the screen is not touched, and the preview updates at once.
layoutSheetContent.example: to stick the Layout at the entrance you turn the measures off and the sheet shows only the zone names; for the construction plan you leave them on.

layoutRotate.what: Rotates the sketch a quarter turn to the right each time you tap it (90°, 180°, 270° and back to the start). Use it to arrange the sketch the way you will print it, for example with the warehouse lying down or standing up. It only turns the drawing: the tables and what is saved do not change, the texts stay upright and the rotation is remembered in this browser. The downloaded sheet comes out with this rotation (you can change it right there for that download only).
layoutRotate.example: the warehouse is long and the sheet is portrait: you rotate the sketch a quarter turn and it fills the sheet better.

layoutCardAlign.what: Choose where the categories go inside the card outline. Top keeps them right under CATEGORY / FIND ME, as always. Centered keeps CATEGORY / FIND ME on top and centers the categories in the space left in the outline; with many categories there is no spare room and it looks the same. It only changes how the card is drawn: each category's QR and what is saved do not change. The PDF and image come out as shown in the preview and the choice is remembered in this browser.
layoutCardAlign.example: the zone only has General Warehouse: with Centered it sits in the middle of the outline instead of stuck to the top with all the empty space below.

layoutSite.what: The name of the place (the site). It appears above the company name in the header of the Layout sheet and of the printed cards. If you leave it empty the usual text is used. Later it will come from settings.
layoutSite.example: you type Chihuahua Distribution Center and the header shows it on top with the company name below.

skuEditar.what: Sends this code to Operations > Code Editing so you can fix it. Here, in Codes, they are only viewed. It is noted in the code history.
skuEditar.example: you got the weight wrong: you choose Edit, fix it in Code Editing and when finished it comes back here.

skuTerminarEdicion.what: Finishes this code editing and sends it back to Catalogs > Codes. It is only possible when the code has all 24 data filled in.
skuTerminarEdicion.example: you fixed the weight and the photos are complete: you choose Finish editing.

layoutZoneUse.what: What the zone is used for, apart from its type (Dry, Refrigerated…): Storage (product is kept), Operations (work happens: receiving, picking, shipping) or Facilities (restroom, pumps, electrical room and other building services). It can be left not set.
layoutZoneUse.example: Zone 1 is Dry and used for Storage; the Restroom is Facilities; the Dock is Operations.

layoutQrBy.what: Choose what to print: the whole Layout (the sheet with the map and the QR, as always) or a Zone (a sheet with the categories of the codes in that zone, each with its QR). It only shows if you have both accesses.
layoutQrBy.example: for the rack in Zone 1 you pick Zone; for the office you pick Layout.

layoutQrZonePick.what: The zone the sheet is made for. The zones of the saved Layout are listed.
layoutQrZonePick.example: you pick Zone 2 and, next to it under Zone type, you see it is Refrigerated.

layoutQrZoneKind.what: The type of the zone you picked (dry, refrigerated, aisle, dock…). Read only: it is changed in the Layout zones table.
layoutQrZoneKind.example: you pick Zone 2 and Refrigerated appears here.

layoutQrZoneType.what: Which of the 7 code categories the list is made from: Inventory, Purchasing, Storage, Rotation, Special handling, Risk or Shelf life. Each code appears under the category written for it in Item Registration. Codes without that category are left out.
layoutQrZoneType.example: with Inventory Category the list says Medications, Wound care and Solutions.

layoutQrZoneSheet.what: Downloads the zone sheet (PDF or image) with the list of categories, how many codes each has and one QR per category. The QRs never change: scanning one always shows what is current, even if the sheet was printed months ago. The list comes from what is saved in Code Relation.
layoutQrZoneSheet.example: you print the Zone 1 sheet on half letter and stick it at the zone entrance.

layoutFilterClear.what: Removes every filter from this table and shows all its rows again. Filters are set with the funnel in each header, like in the other tables.
layoutFilterClear.example: you filtered the Type column to see only aisles; when you are done, Clear filters brings back all the zones.

layoutZoneFmt.what: Opens this zone's format, like Excel's Format Cells: background color, stripes or pattern, and border style and color. Without its own format, the zone uses its type color.
layoutZoneFmt.example: you give the Warehouse purple diagonal stripes and a dashed border to tell it apart from other dry zones.

layoutFmtColor.what: Opens the system color window (the same one used in the trees) to pick this color; the change shows right away in the preview.
layoutFmtColor.example: you pick a light yellow background and an amber for the stripes.

layoutFmtPattern.what: Fill stripes or pattern: diagonal, horizontal, vertical, grid, dots or crossed stripes. Solid is one color and No fill shows what is underneath.
layoutFmtPattern.example: diagonal stripes to mark a zone under construction.

layoutFmtLine.what: Line style of the zone border: solid (thin, medium or thick), dashed, dotted, dash-dot, double or none.
layoutFmtLine.example: a dashed border for a temporary zone.

layoutFmtReset.what: Removes this zone's own format: it goes back to its type color.
layoutFmtReset.example: the zone no longer needs its own color and looks like the other dry zones again.

layoutZonePlanM2.what: The m² your plan states for this room. The system compares what you drew against that number and warns if they differ (more than 3%). It is optional.
layoutZonePlanM2.example: your plan says the Warehouse room is 38.89 m²; if what you drew gives 45 m², it turns amber so you can check the measures.

layoutFreeShape.what: Turns this rectangle into a free-shape zone: it is edited side by side, the way the plan shows it, for L-shaped rooms, notches or slanted walls.
layoutFreeShape.example: the Supplier dock is L-shaped: you switch it to free shape and type its 6 sides.

layoutSidesOpen.what: Shows or hides the sides of this free-shape zone so you can type or fix them.
layoutSidesOpen.example: you tap Sides and change side 3 from 1.27 to 1.30 m.

layoutSideDir.what: Which way this side goes, from the corner where the previous one ends. The diagonal arrows also ask for their tilt.
layoutSideDir.example: Right for a horizontal wall; Right and up for a wall that rises at a slant.

layoutSideTilt.what: How many degrees the side tilts from the horizontal (0.1 to 89.9). It only appears with the diagonal arrows.
layoutSideTilt.example: a wall that rises 30° to the right: you pick Right and up and type 30.

layoutSideLen.what: How long this side is, in meters, as your plan states it.
layoutSideLen.example: 4.57 for the width of the dock.

layoutSideAdd.what: Adds a side at the end. Sides are typed in order, going around the shape on the inside.

layoutSideInsert.what: Adds a side right after this one without touching the others. This side is split into two equal parts and the shape still closes; then you change which way the new part goes or how long it is.
layoutSideInsert.example: you need a notch between side 2 and side 3: you tap + on side 2 and set the new part to Down, 1 m.

layoutSideClose.what: Adds the straight sides that are missing to get back to the corner where you started.
layoutSideClose.example: you are missing 6.30 m to the left and 6.17 m up: one tap adds both sides.

layoutSideCloseLine.what: Closes the shape with a single straight side, from the last corner to the starting one, even if it ends up slanted.
layoutSideCloseLine.example: your last side runs diagonally back to where you started: you close it in one go.

layoutContornoMode.what: How you enter the outline: by sides (which way it goes and how long, as the plan shows it) or by corners (their X and Y meters).
layoutContornoMode.example: with the plan at hand you use By sides; if you already have coordinates you use By corners.

layoutOrigin.what: Where on the map the first corner is; the sides are drawn from there.

layoutCanvas.what: The map of the warehouse, drawn by itself from the data you enter: walls, zones, racks, doors and power connections.
layoutCanvas.example: you change the width of a zone and the map updates instantly.

layoutSave.what: Saves the Layout with all the changes. Until you save, only you can see them.
layoutSave.example: you finish entering the doors and save so others can see the Layout.

layoutDiscard.what: Undoes the changes you have not saved and goes back to the last saved Layout.
layoutDiscard.example: you entered something by mistake and go back to how it was.

layoutSummary.what: A summary of each zone: its name and its zone type (each in its own column), its m², how many spaces it has, how much floor they take and how many storage m³ there are.
layoutSummary.example: you see that Zone A is 25% occupied by its racks.

layoutPlanWidth.what: The real width of the plan, in meters. With it the system knows the scale to draw your warehouse over the plan.
layoutPlanWidth.example: the plan is 48 meters wide and you type it in.

layoutQrMenu.what: Downloads the Layout sheet with the map and the QR, or copies the QR link. The QR never changes and always opens the latest saved Layout.
layoutQrMenu.example: you download the sheet, print it and stick it at the warehouse entrance.

layoutQrPdf.what: Opens the window to download the sheet as a PDF: there you choose the size (A3, A4, Letter, Half letter, Card or any width and length in cm), see how it will look and download it with the map, the KPIs and the QR, ready to print. The sheet comes out as you see the sketch: if you hid the measures or left only some steps active (doors, power, zones...), it only has that. It has what was last saved.
layoutQrPdf.example: you leave only Zones active, hide the measures and the sheet comes out with only the zones, no doors or measures.

layoutQrPng.what: Opens the same window to download the sheet as an image, at the size you choose, to send by message or email. It comes out as you see the sketch (same layers and measures). It has what was last saved.
layoutQrPng.example: you send it by message to a supervisor.

layoutQrLink.what: Copies the address the QR carries, in case you need it somewhere it will not be printed.
layoutQrLink.example: you paste it in an email so it can be opened from a phone.

layoutQrRegen.what: Replaces the QR with a new one. The old one stops working and the sheets have to be printed again. Use it only if the QR left the company.
layoutQrRegen.example: someone photographed the QR outside the warehouse and you prefer to cancel it.

sidebarFlyoutSection.what: This is the name of the section you hovered over. Its options unfold once you reach it; a click opens the sidebar with the section expanded.
sidebarFlyoutSection.example: with the sidebar closed you hover the Customer Service icon, reach its name and pick Our Customers without opening the sidebar.

genericActions.what: This is where the buttons to edit, delete, or do something else with this record live.
genericActions.example: you tap the pencil icon in this column to edit that row.

genericUsername.what: The username this person uses to log in to the system.
genericUsername.example: "admin_saas" is what that person types on the login screen, along with their password.

genericEmail.what: The email address registered for this account.
genericEmail.example: the system uses this email if this person needs to recover their access.

genericCreatedAt.what: The date this record was created.
genericCreatedAt.example: you see how long this account or record has existed in the system.

genericStatus.what: Says what state this record is in right now (for example, Active or Inactive).
genericStatus.example: you see at a glance whether this account is still active, without opening it.

genericName.what: The name that identifies this record.
genericName.example: you see the name this row is known by in the list.

createNewRecord.what: Creates a new record for this list, ready to fill in.
createNewRecord.example: you tap this button to add a new client, item, or record to the list.

genericColumnHeader.what: This column shows "{name}" for every record. Click the title to sort the table by it, drag it to move the column, and use the funnel to filter by this column.
genericColumnHeader.example: to find a record quickly, filter "{name}" by typing part of its value.

genericColumnCell.what: This is the "{name}" of this record.

savedLayout.what: Opens your list of saved layouts: pick one and the table rearranges instantly, or add a new one. While one is applied, its name is written on this icon.
savedLayout.example: you save "Supervisors view" with only the columns you use and apply it every morning with one click.

savedSearch.what: Opens your list of saved searches: pick one and the table filters instantly, or add a new one by choosing the columns and their filters. While one is applied, its name is written on this icon.
savedSearch.example: you save "Active this month" and apply it every morning with one click.

filterToggle.what: Opens or closes the filter panel above the table, to look for records by several fields at once.
filterToggle.example: you open the panel, pick a Status, tap Search and see only those records.

filterClear.what: Clears every filter and leaves the table as it started: all records and the columns in their original order.
filterClear.example: after searching for one client, you tap Clear to see everyone again.

clearSearch.what: Removes the saved search you have applied and leaves the table with no filters, showing every record.
clearSearch.example: you applied "Active this month" and want to see everything again: tap the ✕.

filterAdvanced.what: Adds more filters to the panel: pick any column of the table and its field shows up here to filter by. You can keep going until every column is included; the ones you add are remembered for this table.
filterAdvanced.example: you want to filter by Contracted Cost besides Plan: tap Advanced filter and pick that column.

filterPanelClear.what: Removes everything filtered, in the panel fields and in the columns, and shows every record again. It does not change the column layout.
filterPanelClear.example: you checked the active clients and want to see them all again.

filterPanelField.what: Filters the table by this column. It applies when you tap Search, like the other panel fields, and it is the same filter as the column header.
filterPanelField.example: you pick the Basic and Professional plans and tap Search.

clearLayout.what: Removes the saved layout you have applied and returns the table to its default layout: the one assigned to you, or the table's original if you have none.
clearLayout.example: you applied "Supervisors view" and want things back as they were: tap the ✕.
